examples: The restaurant is owned by a well-known chef from Chicago.
She is well known for her work on climate policy.
He is better known as a songwriter than as a singer.
It's a well-known fact that smoking causes cancer.
It is well known that the first year of a startup is the hardest.

senses.head: Known about by many people; famous
examples: The restaurant is owned by a well-known chef from Chicago.
She is well known for her work on climate policy.
He is better known as a songwriter than as a singer.

senses.head: Of a fact or idea: known to most people, so that nobody needs to explain it
examples: It's a well-known fact that smoking causes cancer.
It is well known that the first year of a startup is the hardest.

entries.position: both — always hyphenated before a noun (a well-known writer); after a verb often written open (she is well known)
entries.comparison: irregular — better-known, best-known; after a verb better known, best known
entries.takes: for + noun or -ing (the reason people know it); as + noun (the role it is known in); to + person (who knows it); that-clause in it is well known that
entries.contrast: The comparative is better-known, best-known, not weller-known; more well-known is common in speech but is avoided in careful writing. The preposition changes the meaning: well known for her novels (the reason), well known as a novelist (the role), well known to the police (who knows her). A well-known fact is общеизвестный, not just известный, so it needs no famous: say a well-known fact, never a famous fact.

examples: Our neighbors have three very well-behaved kids.
The dog was surprisingly well behaved at the vet.
This year's class is the best-behaved group I've ever taught.
A well-behaved app doesn't drain your battery in the background.
The function is well behaved for all positive values of x.

senses.head: Of a child, student or animal: behaving politely and doing what they are told
examples: Our neighbors have three very well-behaved kids.
The dog was surprisingly well behaved at the vet.
This year's class is the best-behaved group I've ever taught.

senses.head: Of a machine, program or process: working in a predictable way, without surprises
examples: A well-behaved app doesn't drain your battery in the background.
The function is well behaved for all positive values of x.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a well-behaved dog); after a verb often written open (the kids were well behaved)
entries.comparison: irregular — better-behaved, best-behaved; after a verb better behaved
entries.form: compound — well + past participle of behave
entries.contrast: Russian воспитанный about an adult is usually polite or well-mannered; well-behaved is mostly said of children, pets and students, and describes how they act, not their upbringing. The comparative is better-behaved, not more well-behaved in careful writing.

examples: She grew up in a well-off suburb outside Boston.
His parents are pretty well off, so he graduated without loans.
The tax cut mostly helps the best-off households.
You don't know how well off you are with a boss like that.
We'd be better off leaving before the traffic starts.
Honestly, she's better off without him.

senses.head: Having plenty of money; comfortably rich
examples: She grew up in a well-off suburb outside Boston.
His parents are pretty well off, so he graduated without loans.
The tax cut mostly helps the best-off households.

senses.head: In a good or lucky situation
examples: You don't know how well off you are with a boss like that.
We'd be better off leaving before the traffic starts.
Honestly, she's better off without him.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a well-off family); more often after a verb and written open (they're well off); the 'in a good situation' sense only after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better-off, best-off; after a verb better off, best off
entries.takes: in the 'in a good situation' sense, better off often takes -ing or without + noun: You'd be better off taking the bus; She's better off without him
entries.contrast: Better off is the everyday comparative and usually means 'in a better situation', not 'richer': You'd be better off asking your boss = тебе лучше спросить начальника. Well-off is politer than rich and a little less than wealthy. The British well off for (well supplied with: well off for cash) is rare in American English.

entries.meaning: Wearing attractive, stylish or expensive clothes. ---
examples: A well-dressed woman in a gray suit walked into the lobby.
Everyone at the wedding was well dressed except the groom's brother.
The magazine publishes a list of the year's best-dressed celebrities.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a well-dressed man); after a verb often written open (he was well dressed)
entries.comparison: irregular — better-dressed, best-dressed; after a verb better dressed
entries.contrast: Dressed alone only means 'wearing clothes' (Are you dressed yet? = ты оделся?); well-dressed means wearing good, stylish clothes. Say the best-dressed guest, not the most well-dressed guest in careful writing.

entries.meaning: Of a job or a person: earning or paying a lot of money. ---
examples: He left teaching for a well-paid job in software.
Truck drivers are fairly well paid in North Dakota.
Surgeons are among the best-paid workers in the country.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a well-paid job); after a verb often written open (nurses aren't well paid)
entries.comparison: irregular — better-paid, best-paid; after a verb better paid
entries.contrast: Well-paid describes both the job and the person doing it. Well-paying describes only the job or the employer: a well-paying job, but not a well-paying lawyer. Highly paid means the same as well-paid and is common for people: highly paid executives.

examples: California has been trying to build high-speed rail for years.
The suspect led police on a high-speed chase down the interstate.
Every room in the hotel has free high-speed internet.
A high-speed camera caught the moment the balloon burst.
The scientists used high-speed video to study how the bird lands.

senses.head: Moving, working or sending data very fast
examples: California has been trying to build high-speed rail for years.
The suspect led police on a high-speed chase down the interstate.
Every room in the hotel has free high-speed internet.

senses.head: Of a camera or photography: recording in a very short time, so that fast motion can be seen
examples: A high-speed camera caught the moment the balloon burst.
The scientists used high-speed video to study how the bird lands.

entries.position: attributive only — after a verb use fast: a high-speed train, but the train is fast
entries.comparison: not gradable — technical writing has higher-speed, but in everyday English compare with faster
entries.contrast: It goes before a noun: a high-speed chase, not the chase was high-speed, which sounds odd — say the chase was fast. Speed stays singular inside the compound. Russian скоростной интернет is high-speed internet or broadband, never speed internet.

examples: I had a part-time job at a pizza place all through college.
The position is part-time, about twenty hours a week.
The store hired three part-time workers for the holidays.
He's an accountant by day and a part-time musician on weekends.
She was a part-time student while her kids were small.

senses.head: Of a job, course or schedule: for only part of the usual working or study hours
examples: I had a part-time job at a pizza place all through college.
The position is part-time, about twenty hours a week.

senses.head: Of a person: working or studying fewer than the usual hours, or doing something in addition to a main job
examples: The store hired three part-time workers for the holidays.
He's an accountant by day and a part-time musician on weekends.
She was a part-time student while her kids were small.

entries.русский: с неполной занятостью; на неполный рабочий день
entries.position: both — a part-time job; the job is part-time
entries.contrast: In She works part-time the word is an adverb, not an adjective. Russian полставки is part-time or half-time in a job, but halftime on its own is the break in a sports game. The job is part-time, never part-timed; a person who works part-time is a part-timer (noun).

examples: After the internship, they offered her a full-time position.
The program is full-time, so most students don't work.
The company has forty full-time employees.
She became a full-time mom after the twins were born.
Taking care of my dad has become a full-time job.
Keeping that old house in shape is practically full-time work.

senses.head: Of a job, course or schedule: for the whole of the normal working or study week
body: (с полной занятостью, на полный рабочий день)
examples: After the internship, they offered her a full-time position.
The program is full-time, so most students don't work.

senses.head: Of a person: working or studying the full number of hours, or doing something as their main activity
examples: The company has forty full-time employees.
She became a full-time mom after the twins were born.

senses.head: Taking up all your time and energy, in a full-time job
examples: Taking care of my dad has become a full-time job.
Keeping that old house in shape is practically full-time work.

entries.position: both — a full-time job; the job is full-time
entries.contrast: In She works full-time the word is an adverb, not an adjective. Full time as a noun is British sports talk for the end of a match; Americans say the end of regulation or the final whistle. Russian штатный сотрудник is usually a full-time employee or staff member.

examples: Nobody really knows the long-term effects of the drug.
We need a long-term solution, not another quick fix.
The board wants a longer-term strategy for the company.
They've been in a long-term relationship for eight years.
Her grandmother lives in a long-term care facility.
The problem isn't temporary; it's long-term.
Long-term capital gains are taxed at a lower rate.
The city took out a long-term loan to fix the bridge.

senses.head: Planned for, or having effects over, a long time into the future
examples: Nobody really knows the long-term effects of the drug.
We need a long-term solution, not another quick fix.
The board wants a longer-term strategy for the company.

senses.head: Lasting or having existed for a long time
examples: They've been in a long-term relationship for eight years.
Her grandmother lives in a long-term care facility.
The problem isn't temporary; it's long-term.

senses.head: In finance: lasting more than a year before it must be paid or sold
examples: Long-term capital gains are taxed at a lower rate.
The city took out a long-term loan to fix the bridge.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: long-term goals; after a verb: the damage could be long-term
entries.comparison: not gradable — but longer-term is common: a longer-term plan
entries.contrast: In the long term is a noun phrase; Americans more often say in the long run. Long-term is about time into the future or over a long period; long-lasting is about how long a thing keeps working (a long-lasting battery, not a long-term battery). Term stays singular: never long-terms plans.

examples: Cutting prices is only a short-term fix.
The layoffs brought a short-term boost in profits but hurt morale.
Most investors care more about shorter-term returns.
The city is cracking down on short-term rentals.
Alcohol affects your short-term memory.
The side effects are usually mild and short-term.
The company borrowed money with a short-term loan.
Short-term interest rates went up again this month.

senses.head: Planned for, or having effects over, only the near future
examples: Cutting prices is only a short-term fix.
The layoffs brought a short-term boost in profits but hurt morale.
Most investors care more about shorter-term returns.

senses.head: Lasting only a short time
examples: The city is cracking down on short-term rentals.
Alcohol affects your short-term memory.
The side effects are usually mild and short-term.

senses.head: In finance: lasting a year or less before it must be paid or sold
examples: The company borrowed money with a short-term loan.
Short-term interest rates went up again this month.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a short-term contract; after a verb: the effect is only short-term
entries.comparison: not gradable — but shorter-term is used: shorter-term goals
entries.contrast: Short-term describes something planned or meant to last a short time; short-lived describes something that ended sooner than expected (a short-lived marriage). Russian кратковременная память is short-term memory, never short memory.

entries.meaning: Known by people in many countries. ---
examples: The Grand Canyon is a world-famous natural wonder.
The city is world-famous for its jazz clubs.
Stop by Rosa's for her world-famous pecan pie.
entries.position: both — a world-famous pianist; the bakery is world-famous
entries.takes: for + noun or -ing (what it is famous for)
entries.contrast: Learners often say worldwide famous or world famous by — say world-famous for. It is also used jokingly about something only locally known: Joe's world-famous chili.

entries.meaning: Containing no sugar, often sweetened with something artificial instead. ---
examples: Could I get a sugar-free vanilla latte?
The label says the candy is sugar-free, but it still has calories.
Chewing sugar-free gum after meals is good for your teeth.
entries.position: both — sugar-free gum; the soda is sugar-free
entries.contrast: In compounds -free means 'without', not 'at no cost': sugar-free = без сахара, tax-free = без налога. Sugar-free food is usually sweetened with something else; unsweetened means nothing sweet was added, and no sugar added means the food may still contain natural sugar.

entries.meaning: Using the newest and most advanced ideas, methods or technology. ---
examples: The hospital just opened a state-of-the-art cancer center.
The gym's equipment is state of the art.
The team trains in a state-of-the-art facility outside Dallas.
entries.type: compound — phrase used as an adjective
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a state-of-the-art lab); after a verb often written open (the equipment is state of the art)
entries.comparison: not gradable — the most state-of-the-art is heard in advertising but avoided in careful writing
entries.form: compound — noun phrase the state of the art turned into a modifier
entries.contrast: The noun phrase the state of the art means the current level of development in a field: the state of the art in cancer research. The adjective means 'the newest and best'. Russian последнее слово техники is usually state-of-the-art or cutting-edge.

examples: Make sure your résumé is up to date before you apply.
The app gives you up-to-date traffic reports.
This is the most up-to-date map we have.
I try to stay up to date on local politics.
Keep me up to date on how the surgery goes.
Is your dog up to date on its shots?
We're up to date with the rent now.
The kitchen needs more up-to-date appliances.
The school uses fairly up-to-date teaching methods.

senses.head: Containing the latest information
examples: Make sure your résumé is up to date before you apply.
The app gives you up-to-date traffic reports.
This is the most up-to-date map we have.

senses.head: Of a person: knowing the latest news or developments
examples: I try to stay up to date on local politics.
Keep me up to date on how the surgery goes.

senses.head: Done or paid when due, with nothing left overdue
examples: Is your dog up to date on its shots?
We're up to date with the rent now.

senses.head: Modern; using the newest methods, styles or equipment
examples: The kitchen needs more up-to-date appliances.
The school uses fairly up-to-date teaching methods.

entries.type: compound — phrase used as an adjective
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (up-to-date information); after a verb usually written open (the list is up to date)
entries.takes: on or with + noun: up to date on the news (informed about), up to date with your payments or on your shots (not behind)
entries.form: compound — prepositional phrase up to date used as a modifier
entries.contrast: Russian актуальный is up-to-date or current, never actual: actual means 'real' (the actual price = реальная цена). Common verb patterns: keep someone up to date, bring something up to date, stay up to date on.

examples: Our office still runs on out-of-date computers.
The phone number on the website is out of date.
This guidebook is even more out of date than the last one.
You can't fly with an out-of-date ID.
His license was out of date, so he got a ticket.

senses.head: No longer modern, useful or correct because things have changed
examples: Our office still runs on out-of-date computers.
The phone number on the website is out of date.
This guidebook is even more out of date than the last one.

senses.head: Of a document or ticket: no longer valid because the date on it has passed
examples: You can't fly with an out-of-date ID.
His license was out of date, so he got a ticket.

entries.type: compound — phrase used as an adjective
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (out-of-date software); after a verb usually written open (the software is out of date)
entries.form: compound — prepositional phrase out of date used as a modifier
entries.contrast: For passports, credit cards, licenses and food, Americans usually say expired: expired milk, an expired passport; out-of-date milk sounds British. Outdated is a close synonym of the first sense. Russian просроченный is therefore most often expired.

entries.meaning: Done, made, bought or happening at the latest possible time. ---
examples: The mall is full of last-minute Christmas shoppers.
There were a few last-minute changes to the schedule.
We found a last-minute deal on a cruise to Mexico.
entries.русский: сделанный в последний момент; горящий (о туре)
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb use at the last minute: a last-minute change, but the plans changed at the last minute
entries.contrast: After a verb, careful English uses the phrase at the last minute: the plans changed at the last minute; it was all very last-minute is casual speech. Russian горящая путёвка is a last-minute deal. The last minute of the game is an ordinary noun phrase meaning the final sixty seconds.

examples: A middle-aged couple bought the house next door.
Most of the people at the concert were middle-aged.
The drug is tested mainly on middle-aged adults.
Minivans have a middle-aged image he wanted to avoid.
Staying home on Friday night feels so middle-aged.

senses.head: Of a person: no longer young but not yet old, roughly between 45 and 65
examples: A middle-aged couple bought the house next door.
Most of the people at the concert were middle-aged.
The drug is tested mainly on middle-aged adults.

senses.head: Typical of middle-aged people, especially in being dull or conservative
examples: Minivans have a middle-aged image he wanted to avoid.
Staying home on Friday night feels so middle-aged.

entries.русский: средних лет; для людей средних лет
entries.type: compound — adjective + -ed from age; also age
entries.position: both — a middle-aged man; my parents are middle-aged
entries.comparison: not gradable — informal more middle-aged is possible in the 'unexciting' sense
entries.form: compound — middle + aged (adjective from the noun age)
entries.contrast: Middle-aged has nothing to do with the Middle Ages: Russian средневековый is medieval. Here aged is one syllable /eɪdʒd/; the separate adjective aged meaning 'very old' (aged parents) is two syllables /ˈeɪdʒɪd/. Middle-aged usually means about 45 to 65.

examples: About one in ten people is left-handed.
The Dodgers need another left-handed pitcher.
Do you have any left-handed scissors?
He learned to play on a left-handed guitar.
"You look great for your age" is a left-handed compliment.
Calling her essay "surprisingly good" was a pretty left-handed compliment.
The left pedal has a left-handed thread, so you loosen it clockwise.
Some gas fittings use left-handed threads so they can't be mixed up.

senses.head: Of a person: using the left hand more easily than the right
examples: About one in ten people is left-handed.
The Dodgers need another left-handed pitcher.

senses.head: Made for, or done with, the left hand
body: (для левой руки, для левшей; левой рукой)
examples: Do you have any left-handed scissors?
He learned to play on a left-handed guitar.

senses.head: Of a compliment: seeming to praise but really meant as criticism
examples: "You look great for your age" is a left-handed compliment.
Calling her essay "surprisingly good" was a pretty left-handed compliment.

senses.head: Of a screw thread: tightened by turning counterclockwise
examples: The left pedal has a left-handed thread, so you loosen it clockwise.
Some gas fittings use left-handed threads so they can't be mixed up.

entries.position: both — a left-handed pitcher; she is left-handed
entries.contrast: Russian левша is a noun, but English usually uses the adjective: She is left-handed, not She is a left-handed; the nouns are a left-hander or informal a lefty. Left-hand without -ed means 'on the left': the left-hand lane. A left-handed compliment (US) is a remark that sounds nice but is really an insult.

examples: I'm right-handed, but I kick with my left foot.
The Cubs are facing a right-handed pitcher tonight.
Most golf clubs in the store are right-handed.
Desks with a right-handed writing surface are hard for lefties.
Almost every bolt you buy has a right-handed thread.
The right pedal is right-handed, so it loosens counterclockwise.

senses.head: Of a person: using the right hand more easily than the left
examples: I'm right-handed, but I kick with my left foot.
The Cubs are facing a right-handed pitcher tonight.

senses.head: Made for, or done with, the right hand
examples: Most golf clubs in the store are right-handed.
Desks with a right-handed writing surface are hard for lefties.

senses.head: Of a screw thread: tightened by turning clockwise, as most are
examples: Almost every bolt you buy has a right-handed thread.
The right pedal is right-handed, so it loosens counterclockwise.

entries.position: both — a right-handed batter; most people are right-handed
entries.contrast: Right-hand without -ed means 'on the right' (the right-hand side), and your right-hand man is your most trusted helper, not someone who uses the right hand. Russian правша is a noun, but English says He is right-handed; the noun a right-hander is used mostly in sports.

entries.meaning: Attractive in appearance, of a person or sometimes a thing. ---
examples: Her brother is a very good-looking guy.
That's a good-looking truck — is it new?
He's even better-looking in person than on TV.
entries.type: compound — adjective + present participle; also evaluative
entries.position: both — a good-looking guy; he's really good-looking
entries.contrast: Good-looking is about how attractive someone is by nature; looking good (verb + adjective) is about how they look right now: You're looking good! = отлично выглядишь. Good-looking suits men and women; handsome is mostly for men and pretty mostly for women. The comparative is better-looking, not more good-looking.

examples: My dad is easy-going about most things except grades.
She's one of the most easy-going people I've ever worked with.
We need an easy-going dog that's good with kids.
The town has an easy-going beach atmosphere.
The office is easy-going, and nobody wears a tie.

senses.head: Of a person: relaxed, not easily upset, worried or annoyed
examples: My dad is easy-going about most things except grades.
She's one of the most easy-going people I've ever worked with.
We need an easy-going dog that's good with kids.

senses.head: Of a place, pace or style: relaxed and informal
examples: The town has an easy-going beach atmosphere.
The office is easy-going, and nobody wears a tie.

entries.type: compound — adjective + present participle; also quality
entries.position: both — an easy-going boss; my roommate is pretty easy-going
entries.contrast: American dictionaries usually spell it as one word, easygoing; the hyphen is also seen. Russian лёгкий человек is easy-going or easy to get along with, never an easy person or she is easy, which can sound insulting about a woman.

entries.meaning: Willing to listen to and consider ideas and ways of life different from your own. ---
examples: My grandparents are surprisingly open-minded about politics.
An open-minded hiring manager will look past the gap in your résumé.
Travel has made her more open-minded toward other cultures.
entries.position: both — an open-minded teacher; try to be open-minded
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing (the subject); toward + noun (people or ideas)
entries.contrast: Russian открытый человек usually means sociable or frank: outgoing, open or friendly. Open-minded means willing to accept new ideas and people without prejudice.

entries.meaning: Tending to forget things or not notice what you are doing because you are thinking about something else. ---
examples: My absent-minded uncle once drove home without his wife.
I'm so absent-minded lately that I left my keys in the fridge.
He's gotten more absent-minded since he started the new job.
entries.position: both — an absent-minded professor; he's getting absent-minded
entries.contrast: Absent alone means 'not present' (отсутствующий): absent from school. Russian рассеянный about a person is absent-minded; about light it is diffuse or scattered.

entries.meaning: Extremely sad, especially because someone you love has left you or died. ---
examples: She was broken-hearted when her dog died.
The song is about a broken-hearted cowboy.
Fans were broken-hearted over the team's move to another city.
entries.type: compound — past participle + noun + -ed; also emotion
entries.position: both — a broken-hearted widow; she was broken-hearted
entries.comparison: more/most — more broken-hearted, most broken-hearted; rare — usually strengthened with completely or absolutely
entries.contrast: Heartbroken means the same and is more common in everyday American English; broken-hearted sounds a little more literary. The noun phrase is a broken heart: He has a broken heart = He is broken-hearted.

entries.meaning: Having a kind and caring nature. ---
examples: A kind-hearted stranger paid for our groceries.
Deep down, he's gentle and kind-hearted.
She's the most kind-hearted person in our family.
entries.position: both — a kind-hearted nurse; he's kind-hearted
entries.contrast: Kind can describe one action (That was kind of you); kind-hearted describes a person's character. Do not confuse either with kind of, which means 'somewhat' (kind of tired).

examples: Her parents still have an old-fashioned TV with an antenna.
That hairstyle looks a little old-fashioned now.
Call me old-fashioned, but I think you should write a thank-you note.
My grandfather is more old-fashioned about dating than my dad.
The diner still makes old-fashioned milkshakes.
What this team needs is some good old-fashioned defense.

senses.head: No longer modern or in fashion
examples: Her parents still have an old-fashioned TV with an antenna.
That hairstyle looks a little old-fashioned now.

senses.head: Of a person or their views: following traditional ideas about how people should live and behave
examples: Call me old-fashioned, but I think you should write a thank-you note.
My grandfather is more old-fashioned about dating than my dad.

senses.head: Traditional in a good way, like things used to be
examples: The diner still makes old-fashioned milkshakes.
What this team needs is some good old-fashioned defense.

entries.type: compound — adjective + past participle; also evaluative
entries.position: both — an old-fashioned phone; his ideas are old-fashioned
entries.contrast: It can be praise: good old-fashioned hard work = старый добрый упорный труд. An Old Fashioned (no hyphen, capitalized) is a noun — a whiskey cocktail. Old alone is about age; old-fashioned is about style or ideas.

examples: He showed up in a brand-new pickup truck.
The shoes are brand new — I've never worn them.
The network is launching a brand-new comedy series this fall.
Go easy on her; she's brand new here.
The brand-new coach hasn't picked a starting quarterback yet.

senses.head: Completely new: never used before, or only just made or launched
examples: He showed up in a brand-new pickup truck.
The shoes are brand new — I've never worn them.
The network is launching a brand-new comedy series this fall.

senses.head: Of a person: having only just started or arrived
examples: Go easy on her; she's brand new here.
The brand-new coach hasn't picked a starting quarterback yet.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a brand-new car); after a verb often written open (the car is brand new)
entries.contrast: Word order matters: a brand-new car = новенькая машина; a new brand of car = новая марка машины. Brand here is the old word for a burning piece of wood (as new as metal fresh from the fire), not the modern 'company brand'.

examples: My so-called best friend didn't even come to my party.
These so-called diet pills are a waste of money.
The so-called experts got the election completely wrong.
The disease hits hardest in the so-called Stroke Belt of the South.
The bill targets so-called forever chemicals in drinking water.

senses.head: Used to show that you think a name or description is wrong or not deserved
examples: My so-called best friend didn't even come to my party.
These so-called diet pills are a waste of money.
The so-called experts got the election completely wrong.

senses.head: Used neutrally to introduce the name that is commonly used for something
examples: The disease hits hardest in the so-called Stroke Belt of the South.
The bill targets so-called forever chemicals in drinking water.

entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also evaluative
entries.position: attributive only — my so-called friends; after a verb say what is called or known as
entries.contrast: Russian так называемый is often neutral, but English so-called usually shows doubt or sarcasm: the so-called experts means you don't think they are experts. For a neutral term, known as or what is called is safer. Do not add quotation marks as well: the so-called experts, not the so-called "experts".

examples: You can't turn left there; it's a one-way street.
Most of the streets downtown are one-way.
A one-way ticket to Denver costs almost as much as a round trip.
She booked a one-way flight and never came back.
The meeting was a one-way conversation — the boss talked and we listened.
Police watched the interview through a one-way mirror.

senses.head: Of a street or traffic: moving in only one direction
examples: You can't turn left there; it's a one-way street.
Most of the streets downtown are one-way.

senses.head: Of a ticket, fare or trip: for traveling to a place but not back
examples: A one-way ticket to Denver costs almost as much as a round trip.
She booked a one-way flight and never came back.

senses.head: Going or working in one direction only; not shared by both sides
examples: The meeting was a one-way conversation — the boss talked and we listened.
Police watched the interview through a one-way mirror.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a one-way street; after a verb: this street is one-way
entries.contrast: Americans buy a one-way ticket and a round-trip ticket; the British single and return sound foreign in the US. Like every number compound, the noun inside stays singular: a one-way street, a five-year plan, a ten-dollar bill, never a five-years plan. A one-way street is also a noun phrase for a relationship where only one side gives.

examples: He got a free upgrade to a first-class seat.
First-class passengers board before everyone else.
The hospital has a first-class heart surgery team.
The food was good, but the service was first-class.
A first-class stamp covers a letter up to one ounce.
Send the check by first-class mail.

senses.head: Of travel: in the most expensive and comfortable section of a plane or train
examples: He got a free upgrade to a first-class seat.
First-class passengers board before everyone else.

senses.head: Excellent; of the highest quality
examples: The hospital has a first-class heart surgery team.
The food was good, but the service was first-class.

senses.head: Of US mail: in the standard class used for letters and small packages
examples: A first-class stamp covers a letter up to one ounce.
Send the check by first-class mail.

entries.position: both — the travel and mail senses mostly before a noun (a first-class seat); 'excellent' in both positions (the service was first-class)
entries.contrast: In We flew first class the words are an adverb phrase, usually without a hyphen. Russian первоклассник is a first grader, not a first-class student, which would mean an excellent student. First-rate is a synonym of the 'excellent' sense.

examples: We furnished our first apartment with second-hand furniture.
Most of the textbooks I bought were second-hand.
There's a great second-hand bookstore near campus.
The report is based on second-hand accounts from neighbors.
My knowledge of the war is all second-hand.
Second-hand smoke is dangerous for young children.
Watching his awkward speech gave me second-hand embarrassment.

senses.head: Owned or used by someone else before; not new
examples: We furnished our first apartment with second-hand furniture.
Most of the textbooks I bought were second-hand.
There's a great second-hand bookstore near campus.

senses.head: Of information: heard from other people, not seen or learned directly
examples: The report is based on second-hand accounts from neighbors.
My knowledge of the war is all second-hand.

senses.head: Reaching you because of what other people do, especially in second-hand smoke
examples: Second-hand smoke is dangerous for young children.
Watching his awkward speech gave me second-hand embarrassment.

entries.position: both — a second-hand car; all her furniture is second-hand
entries.contrast: American dictionaries and most US writing spell it as one word, secondhand. In I bought it second-hand it is an adverb. Russian секонд-хенд (the store) is a thrift store or a secondhand store in American English — a second-hand alone is not a noun. The second hand (two words) is the hand on a clock that counts seconds.

examples: He trained for years as a long-distance runner.
Long-distance truck drivers spend weeks away from home.
The airline is adding more long-distance flights to Asia.
In the '80s, a long-distance call to Grandma was a big deal.
Is it still long-distance if you call from a cell phone?
They had a long-distance relationship all through college.
Keeping a long-distance friendship going takes effort.

senses.head: Traveling or covering a long distance
examples: He trained for years as a long-distance runner.
Long-distance truck drivers spend weeks away from home.
The airline is adding more long-distance flights to Asia.

senses.head: Of a phone call: between places far apart, usually costing more
examples: In the '80s, a long-distance call to Grandma was a big deal.
Is it still long-distance if you call from a cell phone?

senses.head: Of a relationship: between people who live far away from each other
examples: They had a long-distance relationship all through college.
Keeping a long-distance friendship going takes effort.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a long-distance runner; after a verb in US speech: Is the call long-distance?
entries.contrast: In call long-distance it is an adverb. Russian дальнобойщик is a long-haul trucker or long-distance trucker. Working from home far away is remote work, not long-distance work. Russian отношения на расстоянии is a long-distance relationship.

entries.meaning: Sure of your own abilities and value. ---
examples: She's a self-confident young woman who isn't afraid to speak up.
He seemed relaxed and self-confident in the interview.
Playing on a team made my son much more self-confident.
entries.position: both — a self-confident speaker; she's very self-confident
entries.contrast: Self-confident is praise = уверенный в себе. Russian самоуверенный is criticism and is overconfident, cocky or arrogant in English. Do not confuse it with self-conscious, which means shy and worried about how you look to others (стеснительный).

entries.meaning: Taking a lot of time to do. ---
examples: Refinishing the floors was a long, time-consuming job.
Applying for a visa is expensive and time-consuming.
Grading essays is the most time-consuming part of teaching.
entries.position: both — a time-consuming process; the paperwork is time-consuming
entries.form: compound — noun time + consuming (what it uses up)
entries.contrast: It means 'taking a lot of time', not 'wasting time': a time-consuming job can be worth it. It often comes in it is time-consuming to + verb. Russian трудоёмкий stresses effort, and English may need labor-intensive instead.

entries.meaning: Putting a lot of effort and care into work.
examples: The town is full of hard-working families.
My grandmother was honest and hard-working her whole life.
He's the hardest-working guy on the crew.
entries.type: compound — adjective + present participle; also quality
entries.position: both — a hard-working student; her parents are hard-working
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — harder-working, hardest-working; more hard-working, most hard-working
entries.contrast: American dictionaries usually spell it as one word, hardworking. The superlative is usually hardest-working (the hardest-working man in show business), though most hardworking is also correct. The adjective describes a person; the verb phrase is work hard (adverb): She works hard = She is hard-working = She is a hard worker. Hardly working is a joke meaning 'almost not working'.
